extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, federal judges, and law students studying equity patent practice
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and substantive standards governing hearings, evidence, precedential effect, interlocutory decrees, masters, juries, and appeals in United States equity suits for patent infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of hearing in equity patent actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The hearing of an action in equity for infringement of a patent may take place before one judge sitting alone, before several judges sitting together, before a judge and a jury, or before a master in chancery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges constitute the best tribunals for the purpose; however, other methods of trial may be resorted to at the will of the court, so law relevant to all three methods is outlined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of interlocutory hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: An interlocutory hearing in a patent action in equity occurs after the evidence relevant to the validity of the patent and its infringement has been taken, and before the case is referred to a master to take and state an account of profits and damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The interlocutory hearing is generally the pivotal point of litigation; if it results in dismissal it becomes a final hearing. Final hearings follow after the master's report and generally involve the correctness of that report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on complainant discontinuing at hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: A complainant cannot discontinue his action in equity for infringement when it is called for a hearing without showing some better reason for wishing so to do than an intention to begin a new suit for the same cause and a hope of proving a stronger case in the new suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court will examine all patentability and construction questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of the patentability of inventions and the construction of patents concern the public, and courts will examine all the questions involved in patent cases brought on for hearing and will not refrain from so doing at the suggestion of either party or both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of law and precedential hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of law in equity patent cases are to be decided according to relevant rules of law and equity: United States statutes, decisions of the U.S. Supreme Court, Courts of Appeals, Circuit Courts, District Courts, and decisions of the chancellors of England made before the adoption of the U.S. Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later English decisions may indicate the law but are not binding; decisions of U.S. courts at higher levels are generally binding on lower courts; state court decisions are in the same category as modern English decisions except where federal statutes direct the Federal courts to follow state laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to follow English decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Later decisions of English courts sometimes indicate what the law is, but no such decision is of any binding authority in any United States court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an English decision is strictly relevant to the question at bar and is supported by good reasoning, it may be followed by a U.S. judge; but if it refers to a substantially different state of statute law or was fallaciously reasoned, it may properly be disregarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: State court decisions and federal statute exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The decisions of State courts fall in the same category as modern English decisions, except in cases where United States statutes direct the Federal courts to follow the laws of the several States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In those cases, the State laws are binding on Federal judges because the national legislature has adopted those State laws instead of framing corresponding regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty when no direct authority exists
rubrics_metrics.description: When a question arises to which no direct answer can be found in recognized sources of law, it is the duty of the judge to deduce a proper answer by means of just reasoning from general principles of law, equity, and justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judge may consult obiter dicta and commentators for assistance, but no obiter dictum or textbook is of binding authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedential effect of conflicting Supreme Court decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Points of law actually decided by the U.S. Supreme Court are generally binding on all other U.S. courts, with an exception where the Supreme Court has decided the same question both ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the later decision expressly overruled the first, the last decision governs; if it simply ignored the first, a District Court should probably follow the more reasonable of the two regardless of seniority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binding effect of Circuit Court of Appeals and District Court rulings
rubrics_metrics.description: Points of law decided by the Circuit Court of Appeals of any circuit are binding upon all District Courts in that circuit but not on courts in other circuits; points decided by any District Court judge are followed by other District Judges unless reversed by a Circuit Court of Appeals or the Supreme Court or contrary to higher decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points of law include the construction given to letters patent when the evidence of prior art and other facts remain unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjudicated cases binding only for questions actually submitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudicated cases are binding precedents only where the questions of law involved were actually submitted for decision in those cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raising questions in pleadings without submitting them at hearing, or abandoning questions at hearing, does not create a binding submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions of fact depend on the evidence presented
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of fact depend upon the evidence in the particular cases in which they arise and often require logical reasoning from the record's testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where evidence in multiple District Court cases is substantially the same, other District Courts are apt to follow a carefully argued and deliberately decided case, except when different evidence requires a different decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comity vs. duty to decide rightly
rubrics_metrics.description: While securing uniformity of decision is important and comity suggests following co-ordinate tribunals, it remains the duty of every judge to decide cases according to his own convictions rather than according to other judges; comity properly operates only in cases of doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some circuits have expressed this rule strongly, but judges must decide what they think right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of conflicting Circuit decisions across circuits
rubrics_metrics.description: When one Circuit Court of Appeals holds a patent invalid and another holds it valid, practical questions arise about the effect of decrees rendered in each circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A decree holding a patent valid may except from its operation articles acquired from defendants in circuits where the patent was held invalid; courts have held such decrees should not permit use or sale in the second circuit, though authorities vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binding nature of prior factual determinations by appellate courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a question of fact in a patent case has been decided by a Circuit Court of Appeals, that decision is binding in District Courts of the same circuit when the evidence is substantially the same and will be followed in later suits even if the claim of invalidity was not urged on prior appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the Supreme Court decided a question of fact, that decision is conclusive in subsequent patent cases so far as the evidence is substantially identical, but the evidence must be taken in the subsequent cases and cannot be imported from the higher court's record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collusive or non-adversary prior proceedings not binding
rubrics_metrics.description: Points stated in prior litigated cases apply only to cases litigated in earnest between opposing parties and do not apply to cases collusively conducted or which ceased to be adversary actions before the hearing resulting in the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence complainant must produce in equity patent suits
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence required from a complainant in equity is the same as in an action at law, except equity requires evidence to excuse delay (laches), danger of infringement may substitute for proof of actual infringement, equity courts may take notice of their own records to ascertain prior art, and prior to the interlocutory hearing complainant need not introduce evidence relevant to profits, damages, or notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence to establish infringement must be convincing; a single act showing danger of further infringement may suffice in some circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection of defendant's doings (discovery by inspection)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the complainant has some evidence tending to show that the defendant's doings infringe the complainant's patent, a court of equity has power to order the defendant to allow inspection by the complainant or his representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This power will not be exercised where the bill is filed upon a conjecture of infringement hoping to obtain evidence later; mere suspicion is not sufficient to justify inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of failure to specifically deny averments
rubrics_metrics.description: All averments of a bill not specifically denied, except allegations of the amount of damage, are deemed admitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standards for common and equity-specific defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence required to support the twenty-eight defenses common to actions at law and in equity is the same in both forms; of equity-specific defenses, non-jurisdiction seldom requires evidence, and laches is prima facie supported by the long lapse of time deducible from the complainant's proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the complainant introduces evidence to excuse delay, the defendant may need to negate that evidence or prove facts showing the excuse to be invalid or insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of taking testimony in equity patent causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony in patent causes in equity, as in other equity actions, is generally taken orally in open court, with certain exceptions; the court rules on admissibility of evidence as in an action at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evidence is offered and excluded and exception taken, the court must take and report so much as will clearly show the character, the form offered, the objection, the ruling and the exception; appellate courts will not reverse unless material prejudice results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositions useable by court in special instances
rubrics_metrics.description: In special instances, upon application of either party when allowed by statute or for good and exceptional cause, the court may permit depositions of named witnesses to be used before the court or upon a reference to a master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such depositions may be taken before an examiner or other named officer upon terms specified in the order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for expert testimony by affidavit in patent/trademark cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases involving validity or scope of a patent or trademark, the district court may order that testimony in chief of expert witnesses (matters of opinion) be set forth in affidavits filed on a schedule (plaintiff within 40 days after cause at issue; defendant within 20 days after plaintiff; rebutting within 15 days after defendant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the opposite party desires production of any affiant for cross-examination, the court shall direct cross-examination; unless the affiant is produced and submits to cross-examination the affidavit shall not be used as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of depositions taken in other cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Depositions taken in any other case may be used in an action in equity if each party in the new action was a party to the action in which they were taken, or is in privity with a party thereto, and if the court grants a motion to use them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If either party in the new action was not a party or in privity, no deposition from the former suit can be used against that party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and introduction of documentary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentary evidence is generally introduced before the examiner within the same time oral testimony is required to be taken; each party ought to introduce his documentary evidence when taking his own testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If introduced during the other's testimony it will be treated as if introduced when the introducer was taking his own testimony provided such subsequent taking was proper. Documents proving themselves may be introduced at the hearing without having been put before the examiner; documents requiring proof may be introduced on or after the hearing with consent of the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stipulations binding but withdrawable in limited circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Stipulations are extensively made on undebatable points of fact in patent cases and, when made, are binding upon the parties unless canceled or amended by agreement or court order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will allow withdrawal from an inadvertently made stipulation when it is found to be out of conformity to the truth and when such withdrawal is not unjust to the opposite party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subpoena duces tecum for production of documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a document material to a party's case is known to be in possession of the opposite party, its production in court may be compelled by a subpoena duces tecum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and advisory nature of jury verdicts in equity patent trials
rubrics_metrics.description: A jury of not less than five and not more than twelve may be empanelled in equity for the trial of a patent cause to submit questions of fact; the verdict is treated as in issues sent from chancery and is advisory, never conclusive upon the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the judge disagrees with the jury, he may enter a decree contrary to it; regular course is to enter decree in accordance with the verdict unless a party moves for a new trial. A new trial is granted or refused according to the judge's view of whether the verdict was right. On appeal, the Circuit Court of Appeals will decide whether, on the whole, the decree was right or wrong but will not pass upon correctness of the trial rulings; evidence at jury trial should be preserved for appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and effect of master's report in chancery
rubrics_metrics.description: A master in chancery may be directed, with the consent of the parties, to hear and decide any or all questions in a patent case and to report his decision to the court; such a report is advisory only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions to the master's report are the proper means of appeal. If the judge concludes the master was wrong he may send the case back with directions to make a new report and prescriptions of new criteria, or may proceed to try the questions himself. Rules of practice regulating masters are the same whether ascertaining novelty/infringement or taking accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and limits of interlocutory decree
rubrics_metrics.description: An interlocutory decree in an equity patent case adjudges the patent sued upon is valid, that the defendant has infringed it, and usually directs a master to take an account of profits and damages; sometimes it orders a permanent injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An accounting is not automatic: it may be refused when defendant made only a small number of infringing articles and discontinued infringement before suit and no substantial recovery could be had; accounting may also be denied by reason of laches on the plaintiff's part even if laches insufficient as a defense to injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting limited by actual notice and timing of infringements
rubrics_metrics.description: If a bill prays for an account and actual notice to the defendant is relied on instead of constructive notice (marking), the decree will grant an accounting only as to infringements committed subsequent to receipt of the notice unless post-notice infringements were substantial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may be questionable to decree an accounting at all if it is not shown that there are at least some infringements of which an account could be rendered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial-claim decrees and threshold for judicial relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Where only part of the claims in suit are found valid and infringed, an interlocutory decree is confined to that part; decrees are not entered where the infringement is below the dignity of the court, and such bills are dismissed without costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial destruction of infringing articles is not justified by existing U.S. law, though occasionally mentioned in obiter dicta.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to finding on remaining claims for costs purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the District Court finds certain claims infringed, the defendant is entitled to a finding on the remaining claims in order that he may be relieved from the payment of costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals from interlocutory decrees — timing and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal from an interlocutory decree may in certain cases be taken to the Circuit Court of Appeals for the circuit in which the decree was rendered, at any time within thirty days from the entry of the decree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory changes (notably the 1911 Act effective 1912) extended review jurisdiction to decrees refusing or dissolving injunctions; such appeals secure review of the injunction part and underlying questions of validity and infringement, and the appellate court may decide those questions and direct dismissal if adverse to the complainant. Findings of fact below have great weight on appeal unless obviously erroneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on defendant appeals from decrees ordering accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: No appeal can be taken by a defendant from an interlocutory decree which directs an accounting of profits and damages but does not order an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an interlocutory decree directs an accounting and orders an injunction on only part of the claims, the appellate court will not consider that part of the decree favorable to the defendant, nor any part relating to an accounting.
